definition: A link-state interior routing protocol that floods topology data and runs Dijkstra's algorithm inside each area.
wrongs: A distance-vector protocol that advertises only hop counts.
A path-vector protocol used to exchange routes between autonomous systems.
A hybrid protocol that sends updates only to neighbors when a metric changes.
why: OSPF routers build a link-state database and compute shortest paths; it is carried directly in IP.
example: Campus routers flood link states inside area 0 and each computes its own shortest-path tree.
scenario: A firewall must permit OSPF, which is carried directly in IP. Which IP protocol number should it allow?
scenarioWhy: OSPF uses IP protocol number 89, whereas 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP, and 1 is ICMP.

definition: A group of OSPF routers that share one link-state database; other areas normally attach to backbone area 0.
wrongs: A BGP autonomous system identified by an autonomous system number.
A VLAN that separates broadcast domains on a switch.
A spanning-tree instance that elects one root bridge.
why: Flooding and the link-state database stay inside the area, and area 0 is the backbone that connects other areas.
example: Area 1 and area 2 each keep their own database and both connect to area 0.
scenario: Three OSPF areas are planned. Which area must the others normally attach to so inter-area routes can flow?
scenarioWrongs: Whichever area has the most routers
scenarioWhy: OSPF requires the backbone, area 0, as the area to which other areas normally connect.

definition: A record flooded by OSPF that describes a router's links so neighbors can build the area database.
wrongs: A distance-vector update that carries only a destination and a hop count.
A spanning-tree message that carries a bridge identifier and a path cost.
A BGP keepalive that only confirms a session is alive.
why: Link-state advertisements are the pieces of topology that, once flooded, form the link-state database.
example: A router floods a description of its attached links so every router in the area stores the same topology.
scenario: A router floods a record describing its links so neighbors can build the same area topology database. What is that record?
scenarioWhy: The flooded topology record in OSPF is a link-state advertisement.

definition: Dijkstra's shortest-path calculation that each OSPF router runs on its area link-state database.
wrongs: The Bellman-Ford calculation used by distance-vector protocols such as RIP.
A minimum-spanning-tree algorithm that connects all nodes with least total edge weight.
A hash of the router identifier used only to name the router.
why: From the same area database, Dijkstra's algorithm produces each router's shortest-path tree.
example: After the area database synchronizes, every router independently computes its shortest paths.
scenario: After the link-state database is synchronized, each OSPF router computes its shortest-path tree. Which algorithm does it use?
scenarioWhy: OSPF's SPF calculation is Dijkstra's algorithm, not the distance-vector Bellman-Ford method.

definition: The OSPF router elected on a multiaccess network to originate the network advertisement and reduce adjacencies.
wrongs: The switch elected as the spanning-tree root by the lowest bridge identifier.
The BGP speaker that reflects routes inside an autonomous system.
The host that answers DHCP discovers on a subnet.
why: On a broadcast network the designated router becomes adjacent with the others so they need not all become adjacent with each other.
example: Five routers on one Ethernet elect one designated router instead of forming every possible adjacency.
scenario: Four OSPF routers on one Ethernet LAN have priority 1. Which one becomes the designated router?
scenarioAnswer: The router with the highest router ID
scenarioWrongs: The router with the lowest router ID
The router with the lowest interface cost
The router that sent the first hello
scenarioWhy: When priorities tie, OSPF elects the designated router with the highest router ID.

definition: The OSPF interface metric, commonly derived from bandwidth so a faster link has a lower cost.
wrongs: A value that always equals the number of routers in the path, ignoring speed.
The BGP local preference used to choose an exit from an autonomous system.
The administrative distance that ranks routing protocols.
why: OSPF sums interface costs along a path and prefers the smallest sum, and cost usually falls as bandwidth rises.
example: With cost inverse to bandwidth, a 1 Gbit/s link is preferred to a 100 Mbit/s link on otherwise equal paths.
scenario: Costs are inverse to bandwidth and both paths have two hops. One path is 1 Gbit/s and the other is 100 Mbit/s. Which path does OSPF choose?
scenarioWrongs: The path with higher router IDs
scenarioWhy: A faster link has the lower OSPF cost, so the 1 Gbit/s path is preferred.

definition: A path-vector exterior routing protocol that exchanges reachability between autonomous systems over TCP.
wrongs: A link-state interior protocol that floods LSAs and runs Dijkstra.
A distance-vector interior protocol that uses hop count.
A layer-2 protocol that blocks redundant switch ports.
why: BGP carries routes between autonomous systems and uses the path of systems to prevent routing loops.
example: An ISP edge router maintains BGP sessions with neighboring providers to learn Internet prefixes.
scenario: A firewall must allow BGP sessions. Which transport and port should be permitted?
scenarioWhy: BGP sessions run over TCP port 179.

definition: A set of networks under one routing policy, identified by an autonomous system number.
wrongs: A single OSPF area inside a larger OSPF domain.
A VLAN on one switch.
A collision domain on a hub.
why: Exterior routing treats the whole set as one administrative domain identified by its AS number.
example: A university network uses AS 65001 for every prefix it advertises to its ISP.
scenario: A campus advertises all of its prefixes to providers under the number 65001. What does 65001 identify?
scenarioWhy: The number used when advertising a domain's prefixes to other domains is an autonomous system number.

definition: A BGP session between routers in different autonomous systems.
wrongs: A BGP session between routers that belong to the same autonomous system.
An OSPF adjacency inside one area.
A spanning-tree relationship between two switches.
why: External BGP is how separate autonomous systems exchange routes with each other.
example: AS 65001 peers with the ISP in AS 64500 to send and receive Internet routes.
scenario: AS 65001 peers with the ISP's AS 64500 to exchange Internet routes. Which session type is required between them?
scenarioWhy: Routers in different autonomous systems exchange routes with eBGP.

definition: A BGP session between routers in the same autonomous system.
wrongs: A BGP session between routers in different autonomous systems.
An OSPF adjacency that floods link states.
A default static route toward an ISP.
why: Internal BGP distributes externally learned routes inside the autonomous system, and iBGP routes are not re-advertised to other iBGP peers.
example: Two edge routers in AS 65001 use iBGP so each learns the prefixes the other learned from providers.
scenario: Router C learns a prefix from iBGP peer A. Under the iBGP rule, what may C do with that prefix toward its other iBGP peers?
scenarioWrongs: Advertise it to every iBGP peer
Advertise it with an empty AS path
Convert it to an eBGP default
scenarioWhy: iBGP split horizon stops a router from advertising an iBGP-learned route to other iBGP peers.

definition: The BGP attribute listing the autonomous systems a route has crossed, used for loop detection and path comparison.
wrongs: The OSPF metric summed from interface bandwidth costs.
The list of MAC addresses a frame has passed.
The TCP sequence number of a BGP session.
why: A router rejects a route whose AS path already contains its own AS number, which stops BGP loops.
example: A route returns to AS 65001 with 65001 already in the AS path, so the router discards it.
scenario: A route advertisement returns to AS 65001 and the AS path already contains 65001. What should the router do?
scenarioWrongs: Install it as the best path
Prepend 65001 and forward it to all peers
Convert it to an OSPF internal route
scenarioWhy: BGP discards a route that already lists the router's own autonomous system, preventing a loop.

definition: A logical broadcast domain configured on switches so ports can be grouped apart from their cabling.
wrongs: A physical collision domain created by a hub.
An IP subnet mask written in dotted decimal.
A spanning-tree port that is forwarding.
why: Ports in the same VLAN share a broadcast domain even when other VLANs use the same switch.
example: Staff ports are placed in VLAN 10 and guest ports in VLAN 20 on one access switch.
scenario: Staff PCs must share broadcasts with each other but not with guest PCs on the same switch. Which configuration separates them?
scenarioWhy: Different VLANs are different broadcast domains, even on one switch.

definition: A switch port that carries a single VLAN and typically sends and receives untagged frames.
wrongs: A switch port that carries many VLANs using tags.
A routed port with an IP address and no VLAN membership.
A port that is disabled by spanning tree.
why: An end host usually has no VLAN tag, so its switch port is an access port in one VLAN.
example: A PC on VLAN 20 is attached to an access port that accepts and sends untagged frames.
scenario: A PC should receive only VLAN 20 traffic and should not see VLAN tags. Which switch-port mode should be used?
scenarioWhy: A single untagged VLAN for an end host is an access port.

definition: A switch port that carries traffic for multiple VLANs between switches, usually with VLAN tags.
wrongs: A port that belongs to only one VLAN and does not tag frames.
A hub port that repeats every bit.
A router interface with only a static route.
why: A trunk keeps VLAN identity across the link by tagging frames so the next switch can separate the VLANs.
example: An uplink between two switches carries VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on one cable.
scenario: Two switches must carry VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on one uplink. Which port mode should that uplink use?
scenarioWhy: Multiple VLANs on one inter-switch link require a trunk.

definition: The standard that adds a 4-byte tag, including a 12-bit VLAN id, to tagged Ethernet frames on a trunk.
wrongs: Cisco's older inter-switch tagging method that encapsulates the whole frame.
A point-to-point protocol used on serial WAN links.
A bit-oriented protocol used on leased serial lines.
why: The 802.1Q tag carries the VLAN identifier so a trunk can multiplex many VLANs on one Ethernet link.
example: A trunk frame contains a 4-byte 802.1Q tag whose VLAN id field says VLAN 20.
scenario: A trunk frame needs a standard 4-byte VLAN tag. Which tagging method should be used?
scenarioWhy: The standard 4-byte Ethernet VLAN tag is IEEE 802.1Q.

definition: Layer-3 forwarding that moves packets between VLANs using a router or a multilayer switch.
wrongs: Layer-2 forwarding of frames inside one VLAN.
Blocking a redundant link with spanning tree.
Translating private addresses to a public address.
why: Separate VLANs do not forward to each other at layer 2, so a layer-3 device must route between them.
example: Hosts in VLAN 10 reach hosts in VLAN 20 through a router-on-a-stick subinterface for each VLAN.
scenario: PCs in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on the same switch cannot ping each other. What must be added so they can communicate?
scenarioAnswer: A router or SVI between the VLANs
scenarioWrongs: A hub on one access port
scenarioWhy: Different VLANs communicate only when a layer-3 device routes between them.

definition: A layer-2 protocol that blocks redundant switch ports so a looped Ethernet LAN has one active path.
wrongs: A link-state routing protocol that computes IP shortest paths.
A path-vector protocol used between autonomous systems.
A protocol that resolves IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses.
why: Spanning Tree builds a loop-free tree and places redundant ports in a blocking state.
example: Two cables connect the same pair of switches, and spanning tree blocks one port to stop a broadcast loop.
scenario: Two links connect the same pair of switches and broadcasts start multiplying. Which protocol should block one port?
scenarioWhy: Spanning Tree blocks a redundant layer-2 port to break a switching loop.

definition: The switch elected as the spanning-tree root, chosen by the lowest bridge identifier.
wrongs: The OSPF router elected on a LAN by the highest priority and router ID.
The BGP speaker with the shortest AS path.
The switch port that carries the native VLAN untagged.
why: The bridge identifier is the priority plus the MAC address, and the lowest identifier becomes the root.
example: All switches keep the default priority, and the switch with the lowest MAC address becomes the root.
scenario: Every switch uses the default spanning-tree priority. Which switch becomes the root bridge?
scenarioAnswer: The switch with the lowest MAC address
scenarioWrongs: The switch with the highest MAC address
The switch with the highest IP address
scenarioWhy: With equal priority, the lowest MAC address yields the lowest bridge ID and wins the root election.

definition: A spanning-tree message that advertises bridge identifiers and path costs so switches can build the tree.
wrongs: An OSPF record that describes IP links.
A BGP update that lists reachable prefixes.
An ARP reply that carries a MAC address.
why: Switches compare bridge protocol data units to elect the root and to choose root and designated ports.
example: Each switch sends messages containing the root id and the cost toward the root.
scenario: Switches exchange messages carrying the root id and the path cost to choose root and designated ports. What are those messages?
scenarioWhy: Spanning-tree control messages are bridge protocol data units.

definition: The rapid spanning-tree protocol that converges faster than classic STP using proposal and agreement.
wrongs: Classic STP, which waits through listening and learning before forwarding.
A distance-vector routing protocol.
A VLAN management protocol that advertises VLAN numbers.
why: RSTP replaces the long listening and learning wait with a handshake so alternate ports can forward quickly.
example: After a link failure, the campus tree recovers in about a second instead of waiting roughly 30 to 50 seconds.
scenario: Classic listening and learning timers make failover take about 30 to 50 seconds. Which protocol is chosen to converge in seconds instead?
scenarioWhy: Rapid Spanning Tree removes the long forward delay of classic STP.

definition: Mechanisms that treat some packets preferentially to meet targets for delay, jitter, loss, or bandwidth.
wrongs: Translating private IP addresses to public addresses.
Blocking redundant switch ports to prevent loops.
Resolving domain names to IP addresses.
why: Quality of service classifies traffic and then queues, schedules, or drops it so important flows are protected.
example: Voice packets are forwarded ahead of a backup transfer when an uplink is congested.
scenario: Voice packets must be forwarded ahead of bulk backups when the uplink is full. Which set of mechanisms is needed?
scenarioWhy: Preferential treatment of selected packets under congestion is quality of service.

definition: A QoS architecture that marks packets with a DSCP and applies per-hop behaviors without reserving each flow.
wrongs: A QoS architecture that signals a per-flow reservation end to end.
Best-effort forwarding with no marking and no special treatment.
A constant-bit-rate virtual circuit from ATM.
why: Differentiated Services uses the DSCP in the IP header so each hop can apply a behavior to a traffic class.
example: Routers honor a DSCP that selects a low-latency queue for voice, with no per-call reservation.
scenario: Packets are marked with a DSCP and each router applies a per-hop behavior, with no per-call reservation. Which architecture is this?
scenarioWhy: DSCP marking and per-hop behavior without per-flow reservations is DiffServ.

definition: Delaying excess packets in a buffer so the output rate stays within a configured profile.
wrongs: Dropping or remarking packets that exceed a rate, without buffering them to smooth bursts.
Forwarding every packet immediately in arrival order with no rate limit.
Blocking a switch port to remove a loop.
why: Shaping meters the output and queues bursts so traffic leaves at the contracted rate instead of being dropped.
example: A branch router buffers a file-transfer burst and releases it at 10 Mbit/s toward the provider.
scenario: Excess bursts should be buffered and released gradually so the provider does not drop them. Which treatment is this?
scenarioWhy: Buffering excess traffic to smooth the output rate is traffic shaping.

definition: Measuring traffic against a rate and dropping or remarking packets that exceed it, without smoothing them.
wrongs: Buffering excess packets so they leave later at a smooth rate.
Scheduling stored packets with weights among queues.
Giving strict priority to a voice queue that is already buffered.
why: Policing enforces a rate by acting on excess packets immediately rather than delaying them in a shaping queue.
example: A provider drops packets that exceed the contracted 50 Mbit/s instead of queuing the excess.
scenario: Packets above the contracted rate are dropped at once and are not queued to smooth the flow. Which treatment is this?
scenarioWhy: Dropping excess packets instead of buffering them is traffic policing.

definition: Translating IP addresses in packet headers so hosts can communicate with a different address.
wrongs: Flooding link states and computing shortest paths.
Blocking redundant Ethernet ports.
Tagging frames with a VLAN identifier.
why: NAT rewrites addresses, commonly letting private hosts use a public address when they cross the network edge.
example: Office hosts use 10.0.0.0/8, and the border router rewrites their source to a public address.
scenario: Office hosts use 10.0.0.0/8 and the border router rewrites their source address to a public address. Which function is the rewrite?
scenarioWhy: Rewriting IP addresses between private and public space is network address translation.

definition: A form of NAT that maps many private addresses to one public address using different transport ports.
wrongs: A permanent one-to-one mapping of one private address to one public address.
A pool that gives each inside host its own public address.
Label swapping in an MPLS core.
why: Port address translation, also called NAT overload, distinguishes flows by source port when they share one public address.
example: Two hundred PCs share 203.0.113.5, and the router tracks each flow by its source port.
scenario: Two hundred PCs share one public address, and the router tells their flows apart by source port. Which translation is this?
scenarioWhy: Many private hosts sharing one public address by port number is PAT.

definition: A permanent one-to-one mapping between one private address and one public address.
wrongs: A many-to-one mapping that distinguishes hosts by source port.
Automatic address configuration from a router advertisement.
A filter that denies traffic to a server.
why: The mapping does not change, so outside hosts can always reach the inside host at the same public address.
example: A web server at 10.1.1.10 is always published on the Internet as 203.0.113.10.
scenario: A web server at 10.1.1.10 must always appear on the Internet as 203.0.113.10. Which translation should be configured?
scenarioWrongs: An ACL that denies the server
scenarioWhy: A fixed one-to-one private-to-public mapping is static NAT.

definition: An architecture that centralizes forwarding decisions in a controller, which programs the network devices.
wrongs: A design in which every router independently runs a full routing protocol and no controller programs the tables.
A layer-2 loop-prevention protocol.
A half-duplex Ethernet access method.
why: Software-defined networking separates decision-making from packet forwarding and places the decisions in a controller.
example: Access switches forward according to rules pushed by a central controller instead of each computing routes.
scenario: Forwarding switches do not compute routes themselves; a central controller pushes their forwarding rules. Which architecture is this?
scenarioWhy: A central controller programming the forwarding devices is software-defined networking.

definition: The part of a network that decides how traffic should be forwarded.
wrongs: The part that moves packets using rules that are already installed.
The power supply and fans of a router.
The VLAN used only for switch management traffic.
why: Routing protocols, the controller, and route calculations live in the control plane and produce forwarding rules.
example: A router runs OSPF and builds a routing table, but that calculation is not itself moving user packets.
scenario: A router calculates best paths and builds the routing table, yet this work does not itself move user packets. Which plane is calculating?
scenarioWhy: Deciding the paths and building the table is control-plane work.

definition: The part of a network device that forwards packets using rules the control plane has installed.
wrongs: The part that calculates routes and installs those rules.
The management session an operator uses to configure the device.
The application that generates the user's email.
why: The data plane, or forwarding plane, matches headers and moves packets without recomputing the routing policy.
example: A switch moves a frame from port 3 to port 8 using an already installed forwarding entry.
scenario: A switch moves a frame from port 3 to port 8 using an already installed forwarding entry. Which plane performs that move?
scenarioWhy: Forwarding with an installed rule is the data plane.

definition: A southbound protocol with which an SDN controller installs match-action entries in a switch flow table.
wrongs: An interior link-state routing protocol.
A protocol that negotiates bundled Ethernet links.
A Cisco discovery protocol that identifies neighboring devices.
why: OpenFlow carries flow modifications from the controller to the switch, each with match fields and actions.
example: The controller writes a match on destination IP and an output-port action into the switch flow table.
scenario: A controller installs a match on destination IP and an output-port action in a switch. Which classic SDN protocol carries that instruction?
scenarioWhy: Installing match-action flow entries from a controller is the role of OpenFlow.

definition: A forwarding method that switches packets using short labels instead of a full IP lookup at every core hop.
wrongs: An interior routing protocol that builds a link-state database.
A layer-2 loop-prevention protocol.
An address translation method at the network edge.
why: Multiprotocol Label Switching inserts a label and core routers swap that label to forward the packet.
example: Core routers forward a packet by a short label and do not look up the full destination IP at each hop.
scenario: Core routers forward using a short tag and skip a full destination-IP lookup at each hop. Which technology is this?
scenarioWhy: Label swapping instead of a full IP lookup at each core hop is MPLS.

definition: The path that labeled packets follow through a sequence of MPLS routers from ingress to egress.
wrongs: A spanning tree of switches with one root bridge.
A collision domain on a shared Ethernet segment.
A DHCP lease that binds an address to a host.
why: The label switched path is the route defined by successive labels from the ingress router to the egress router.
example: Labeled packets enter at the campus edge and follow one path through three core routers to the provider egress.
scenario: Labeled packets travel a set sequence of routers from the ingress edge to the egress edge. What is that sequence called?
scenarioWhy: The sequence of MPLS routers a labeled packet follows is a label switched path.

definition: A short identifier in the MPLS shim header that each hop uses to forward and then swap.
wrongs: A 48-bit address of an Ethernet interface.
A 16-bit TCP or UDP port number.
An application cookie stored by a browser.
why: The shim header carries a 20-bit label; a core router looks up that label and swaps it for the next hop.
example: A core router receives label 18, swaps it for label 42, and forwards the packet to the next router.
scenario: Each core hop swaps a 20-bit value in the shim header and forwards on that value. What is the value?
scenarioWhy: The 20-bit value swapped at each MPLS hop is the label.

definition: The Internet Protocol version that uses 128-bit addresses and a simplified header, and has no broadcast.
wrongs: The Internet Protocol version that uses 32-bit addresses written in dotted decimal.
A network-layer protocol from older Novell networks.
An older Apple protocol used on local networks.
why: IPv6 expands the address to 128 bits, simplifies the header, and uses multicast instead of broadcast.
example: A campus plan uses 128-bit addresses written as hexadecimal groups separated by colons.
scenario: The campus plans addresses that are 128 bits long and written in hexadecimal groups. Which protocol is this?
scenarioWhy: 128-bit hexadecimal addresses identify IPv6.

definition: IPv6 address configuration in which a host forms an address from a router advertisement prefix and an interface identifier.
wrongs: Stateful assignment of an address by a DHCPv6 server.
Manual typing of the full address on every host.
IPv4 address leasing with the discover, offer, request, and acknowledge exchange.
why: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration needs a router advertisement for the prefix and does not lease the address from DHCP.
example: A host hears prefix 2001:db8:1::/64 in a router advertisement and creates its own interface address.
scenario: A host hears a router advertisement with prefix 2001:db8:1::/64 and forms its address without a DHCP lease. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Building an address from a router advertisement prefix is SLAAC.

definition: An IPv6 address in fe80::/10 used only on the local link and configured on every interface.
wrongs: A publicly routable IPv6 address from 2000::/3.
A multicast address that begins with ff.
The loopback address ::1.
why: Link-local addresses are required for neighbor discovery and are never forwarded by a router off the link.
example: With no router present, a host still has an fe80:: address for on-link neighbor traffic.
scenario: With no router, a host still has an address beginning with fe80 for on-link neighbors. Which address type is it?
scenarioWhy: Addresses in fe80::/10 used only on the link are link-local addresses.

definition: A publicly routable IPv6 unicast address from the range 2000::/3.
wrongs: An address used only on the local link and beginning with fe80.
A multicast address beginning with ff.
The single loopback address ::1.
why: Global unicast addresses are assigned from 2000::/3 so they can be routed on the public Internet.
example: The address 2001:db8:acad::10 belongs to the global unicast range used in documentation examples.
scenario: Which IPv6 address type is 2001:db8:acad::10, an address from 2000::/3 rather than from fe80::/10?
scenarioWhy: 2001:db8:acad::10 falls in 2000::/3, the global unicast range.

definition: The IPv6 function, carried in ICMPv6, that resolves link-layer addresses and discovers routers on the link.
wrongs: The IPv4 protocol that broadcasts a request to map an IP address to a MAC address.
A legacy protocol that maps a MAC address back to an IPv4 address.
A Windows name service that maps NetBIOS names to addresses.
why: Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement replace ARP, and Router Advertisements support address configuration.
example: An IPv6 host sends an ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation to learn a neighbor's MAC address.
scenario: An IPv6 host needs a neighbor's MAC address and sends an ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation. Which function is it using?
scenarioWhy: ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation is part of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, which replaces ARP.

definition: An ordered list of permit and deny rules that a device applies to packets, using the first match.
wrongs: A list of prefixes and next hops used to forward packets.
A table of MAC addresses learned on switch ports.
A pool of public addresses used for translation.
why: Access control lists are checked in order, and the first matching rule decides whether the packet is permitted or denied.
example: A router drops traffic from 10.1.1.5 because the first matching rule in the list says deny.
scenario: A router checks an ordered list and drops packets from 10.1.1.5 because the first matching rule says deny. Which feature is the list?
scenarioWhy: An ordered permit and deny list applied to packets is an access control list.

definition: An access list that filters only on the source IP address.
wrongs: An access list that can match protocol and source and destination ports.
An access list that creates temporary openings for return traffic of an inside session.
A VLAN filter applied only to switched ports by MAC address.
why: Because a standard list cannot name the destination, it is usually placed close to the destination so it does not block other wanted paths.
example: A list numbered in the standard range permits only source network 10.1.1.0 and ignores destination ports.
scenario: A standard ACL can match only source addresses. Where should it be placed so it does not block a source from other allowed destinations?
scenarioWrongs: On every access port of every switch
scenarioWhy: A standard ACL cannot distinguish destinations, so it is placed near the destination.

definition: An access list that can filter on source and destination addresses, protocol, and port numbers.
wrongs: An access list that can filter only on the source IP address.
A subnet mask that only separates network and host bits.
A wildcard used solely to ignore address bits, with no permit or deny action.
why: Extended entries can name a precise flow, such as TCP to one host and port, so they are often placed near the source.
example: A rule denies TCP from any host to 10.2.2.10 port 23 and permits other IP traffic.
scenario: A rule must deny TCP to 10.2.2.10 port 23 and allow other traffic. Which ACL type can express that?
scenarioWhy: Matching protocol and destination port requires an extended ACL.

definition: A mask in which a 0 bit means the corresponding address bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored.
wrongs: A subnet mask in which a 1 bit marks the network portion and a 0 bit marks the host portion.
A mask of all 1s that ignores every address bit.
A mask of all 0s that matches every address in a /24 when paired with a network number.
why: Access lists and some routing commands use wildcards, which are the bit-wise inverse of the usual subnet mask.
example: To match 192.168.5.0/24 in an ACL, the wildcard is 0.0.0.255.
scenario: An ACL must match every host in 192.168.5.0/24. Which wildcard mask is correct?
scenarioWhy: A /24 ignores the last eight bits, so the wildcard is 0.0.0.255, not the subnet mask.

definition: Using more than one prefix length inside the same network so each subnet can be sized to its host count.
wrongs: Using one classful mask for every subnet in the network.
Giving every subnet the same /24 regardless of how many hosts it has.
Translating private hosts to a public address.
why: Variable-length subnet masks borrow different numbers of bits so a point-to-point link need not waste a large subnet.
example: From 10.5.0.0/16, one LAN uses /26 for 50 hosts and a router link uses /30 for two hosts.
scenario: One subnet needs 50 hosts and another needs 2, and both come from 10.5.0.0/16 with different prefix lengths. Which technique is this?
scenarioWhy: Different prefix lengths inside one network are variable-length subnet masking.

definition: Advertising one aggregate prefix in place of several more specific prefixes that share a common bit pattern.
wrongs: Advertising every specific prefix with no aggregate.
Choosing the most specific matching route when forwarding one packet.
Splitting one prefix into many smaller subnets.
why: A summary reduces routing-table size when the specific networks are contiguous and match the aggregate.
example: The four networks 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.3.0/24 are advertised as 10.1.0.0/22.
scenario: The prefixes 10.1.0.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24, 10.1.2.0/24, and 10.1.3.0/24 should be advertised as one block. Which summary is exact?
scenarioWhy: Those four /24 networks share 22 bits, so the exact summary is 10.1.0.0/22.

definition: Choosing address blocks and prefix lengths to fit host counts, links, growth, and summarization.
wrongs: Writing permit and deny rules for an interface.
Electing a spanning-tree root bridge.
Smoothing voice traffic with a shaper.
why: A design assigns the longest prefix that still holds the required hosts and aligns blocks so they can be summarized.
example: A designer gives router links /30 and a 50-PC LAN a /26, leaving the rest of the block for growth.
scenario: A LAN needs addresses for 50 hosts. Which is the longest IPv4 prefix that still has enough usable host addresses?
scenarioWhy: Fifty hosts need 6 host bits because 2 to the 6th minus 2 is 62, so the longest fit is /26.

definition: The forwarding rule that selects the matching route with the greatest prefix length.
wrongs: The rule that always uses the first route written in the configuration.
The rule that prefers the route learned from the protocol with the lowest administrative distance when prefixes differ.
The rule that load-balances across every matching prefix regardless of length.
why: A more specific prefix is a better description of the destination, so it beats a shorter matching prefix.
example: For 10.1.1.5, the route 10.1.1.0/24 is chosen over 10.0.0.0/8 because /24 is longer.
scenario: The table has 10.0.0.0/8 via router A and 10.1.1.0/24 via router B. Which route is used for 10.1.1.5?
scenarioWrongs: Neither route, because the prefixes differ
scenarioWhy: Both routes match, and the longer prefix, /24, is selected.

definition: A structured process that uses symptoms and layered checks to find where connectivity or performance fails.
wrongs: Adding features to a routing protocol.
Designing a new addressing plan before any failure exists.
Electing a designated router during normal OSPF startup.
why: Methods such as bottom-up, top-down, or divide-and-conquer isolate the failed layer instead of changing many things at once.
example: No one can connect and the switch port link light is off, so the check starts at the cable and port.
scenario: Nobody can connect, and the switch-port link light is off. Using a bottom-up method, which layer should be checked first?
scenarioWhy: A dark link light is a physical symptom, so bottom-up troubleshooting starts at the physical layer.

definition: A diagnostic that sends probes with increasing TTL and lists each hop from the time-exceeded replies.
wrongs: A single echo to the final host that reports only whether that host replies.
A query that resolves a name to an address.
A display of local sockets and their states.
why: The first probe dies at the first router, the next at the second, and each ICMP Time Exceeded reveals a hop.
example: A technician watches TTL 1, 2, and 3 draw the three routers between a PC and a server.
scenario: Probes are sent with TTL starting at 1 and increasing, and each router that expires a probe replies. Which tool is this?
scenarioWhy: Listing hops from increasing TTL and time-exceeded replies is traceroute.

definition: A local ranking of route sources; when the prefixes are equal, the source with the lower distance is installed.
wrongs: The OSPF cost summed along a path.
The rule that selects the longest matching prefix when the prefixes differ.
The BGP AS-path length of one advertisement.
why: Administrative distance compares sources such as static and OSPF only for the same prefix; it is not the path metric.
example: On a Cisco router a static route and OSPF both offer 10.1.0.0/16, and the static route is installed.
scenario: On a Cisco router the same prefix is offered by OSPF and by a static route. Which source is installed?
scenarioWrongs: The route with the larger metric
scenarioWhy: Cisco administrative distance prefers a static route, distance 1, over OSPF, distance 110, for the same prefix.
